# Create a Simple Event Sign-Up Form with GitHub Copilot

> **In short:** GitHub Copilot can draft a basic sign-up form in HTML when you describe the fields you want in plain language. This guide walks you through planning the fields, asking Copilot for the code, and reviewing the result; it does not cover hosting the form online or collecting responses.

Whether you're organizing a workshop, a community club meetup, or a small team outing, a sign-up form saves you from chasing replies in chat threads. With GitHub Copilot — an AI coding assistant that suggests code as you type — you can describe the fields you want in plain language and get a working HTML form back, without a programming degree. This guide is for organizers who'd rather not write code by hand but want a clean, simple form they understand and can change later.

## Before you start

- A free GitHub account, which you can create at github.com. A "GitHub account" is just a login that unlocks GitHub's tools.
- Access to GitHub Copilot. Copilot comes in a free tier with limited features and paid tiers with more. Check GitHub's official pricing page for the current lineup before you start.
- A code editor where Copilot works. Visual Studio Code (often called VS Code) is the free program most beginners use; install it from Microsoft's official site if you don't have it yet.
- About 20–30 minutes for the first run-through. Once you've done it once, future forms take much less time.

## Step 1 — List the fields your form needs

Open any notepad — paper, your phone, or a plain text file — and write down the questions you want to ask. A typical event sign-up needs four to six fields at most: full name, email address, number of guests, any dietary or accessibility needs, and a free-text comment box. Keep it short; every extra field lowers the number of people who finish the form. If your event has multiple sessions or ticket types, add one "session" or "ticket type" field with a small set of options rather than several separate boxes.
💬 Example: Name; Email; Number of guests (1, 2, 3, 4); Session (Friday evening, Saturday morning, Saturday afternoon); Dietary needs (free text).
You'll know it worked when a friend can read your list and immediately understand who the form is for.

## Step 2 — Open your editor and start a new file

Launch VS Code (or your editor of choice) and create a new file. Save it as `signup.html` in a folder you can find again — the `.html` extension is what tells the computer "this is a webpage." Inside the file, type the bare minimum an HTML page needs: an opening tag, a closing tag, and the words "Event sign-up" between them. If you don't have an editor installed, you can also use GitHub's web editor: open a new repository, create a file called `signup.html`, and start typing there. Pick whichever path feels less intimidating — both end in the same place.
💬 Example: `<html>Event sign-up</html>`
You'll know it worked when the file is saved with the `.html` ending and your placeholder text is visible inside it.

## Step 3 — Turn on GitHub Copilot

In VS Code, Copilot usually appears as light gray "ghost text" suggestions just ahead of your cursor as you type. If you see suggestions right away, you're already set up. If not, look in the editor's side bar for an **Extensions** panel, search for the Copilot extension, and install it. If you're using GitHub on the web, look for a Copilot button near the file toolbar — its exact position changes over time, so check GitHub's current documentation if you can't spot it. Sign in with the same GitHub account that has Copilot access, accept any permissions the prompt asks for, and reload once if suggestions don't appear immediately.
💬 Example: After installing the extension, restart VS Code once and watch for gray suggestions to appear as you pause typing.
You'll know it worked when suggestions start to appear in light gray as you pause, or when a Copilot chat panel opens when you ask for one.

## Step 4 — Ask Copilot to write the form

Inside `signup.html`, place your cursor between the opening and closing HTML tags and write a short instruction as a **comment**. A comment is a line the browser ignores but Copilot reads — in HTML it looks like `<!-- your text here -->`. Describe the event name, the fields from your list, and a submit button. Then pause for a couple of seconds. Copilot should suggest a block of code in gray; press the keyboard shortcut it usually shows (often the Tab key) to accept the suggestion, or click an **Accept** button if one appears. If the first draft isn't what you wanted, rephrase your comment with clearer wording and pause again — Copilot responds to clearer instructions with better code.
💬 Example: `<!-- Build a sign-up form titled "Spring Workshop 2026" with fields for name, email, guests (1-4), session dropdown, and a comments box. Add a Submit button. -->`
You'll know it worked when the file contains a full `<form>` block with labels, input boxes, and a submit button — and you can read the labels and recognize your own field list.

## Step 5 — Review what Copilot wrote

Read the code line by line, slowly. You don't need to understand every symbol — just look for your field names, the labels next to each box, and the submit button. If anything is missing, place your cursor where the new field should go, add another short comment asking for it, and pause for Copilot again. If a label says something you don't want, just edit the words inside the quotation marks. Treat the AI like a helpful assistant: a fast first draft, but your eyes are the final check. The browser ignores anything inside `<!--` and `-->`, so comments won't affect what visitors see.
💬 Example: If Copilot forgot the dietary-needs box, type `<!-- add a free-text box for dietary needs -->` on a new line and pause.
You'll know it worked when you can read every label aloud and recognize it as something a real visitor would understand.

## Step 6 — Save the file and open it in a browser

Save the file with Ctrl+S on Windows or Cmd+S on Mac (or use the File menu). Find `signup.html` in your folder and double-click it. Your default web browser will open it, and you'll see your form exactly as a visitor would. Try typing into each box and clicking Submit — nothing will happen yet, because the form isn't connected to anything, and that's expected. This step is purely to confirm that what you see on screen matches what you asked for. If something looks off, go back to the editor, tweak the labels, save again, and refresh the browser.
💬 Example: Type "Maria" in the name box and "maria@example.com" in the email box; both should hold your typing without errors.
You'll know it worked when the form looks clean in the browser, every box accepts typing, and clicking Submit triggers no scary error messages.

## Step 7 — Decide what to do with the form next

A local HTML file is a real form, but it doesn't send responses anywhere yet. To collect sign-ups, you have a few simple options: paste the HTML into a hosted form builder (Google Forms, Tally, or similar — names change, so check what's currently popular), publish the page for free using GitHub Pages (a GitHub feature that turns a repository into a public website), or hand the file to a more technical friend to wire up. Copilot can help with some of these next steps too, but each one is its own mini-project. For now, the saved file on your computer is your completed deliverable.
💬 Example: Search for "free HTML form hosting" or "GitHub Pages signup form" to see current options, then pick whichever matches your comfort level.
You'll know it worked when you have a saved `signup.html` file that opens cleanly in any browser and that you can confidently show someone else.

## Common mistakes

- **Asking for too many fields on the first try.** Start with five or six — long forms lose sign-ups. Add more later if you really need them.
- **Accepting Copilot's first suggestion without reading it.** Always read the labels and field names out loud; the AI sometimes invents field names that sound reasonable but don't match what you actually wanted.
- **Forgetting to save with the `.html` extension.** A file called "signup" without the `.html` ending will not open as a webpage. Double-check the filename before you double-click it.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** Any time a small group needs to collect names or preferences — a kids' party, a neighborhood dinner, a book club meeting — you can spin up a clean sign-up form in under half an hour, without learning to code.
- **For your business or work:** Workshops, training sessions, customer pre-orders, internal team events — the same template scales. You control the wording, the fields, and the look, and you can change them yourself in seconds.
- **If you're just getting started:** Treat this guide as a sandbox. Your first form will be rough; your second will be quick. The real skill is learning to describe what you want clearly enough that Copilot can draft it for you.

## Try it now

Open your notepad app and write down four fields for an event you'd actually run — a lunch, a class, a playdate — then start a new `signup.html` file in VS Code (or at github.com) and ask Copilot for those exact four fields. Twenty minutes from now you'll have a working sign-up form on your desktop that you can show a friend.
